pages.title: Ken Page on Discouragement Fatigue and the Wave of Distancing
pages.short_answer: On episode 106 of Christina Weber's podcast, psychotherapist Ken Page, author of Deeper Dating, names the two patterns that most derail people looking for love: discouragement fatigue and the wave of distancing. His fix is to measure progress by whether you're becoming more self-treasuring, vulnerable, and discriminating, and to keep asking one question: does my soul feel safe with this person?
pages.meta_description: Ken Page, author of Deeper Dating, on discouragement fatigue, the wave of distancing, and the one question to date by. Key ideas and quotes from episode 106.
pages.content_html:
Ken Page, LCSW, is a psychotherapist, the author of Deeper Dating, host of the Deeper Dating Podcast, and a member of WeDeepen's faculty. Christina Weber calls him one of her mentors in love: "I go to him all the time when I need relationship advice." In episode 106 of her podcast, he named the two patterns he sees derail people looking for love most often, and what to do about each. This guide sums up that conversation. Quotes are from the episode transcript, lightly edited for readability.

Discouragement fatigue

Ken once asked everyone on his email list where they get most stuck in dating. More than a hundred people answered, and he sent each a personal voice message back. One woman named the problem in two words: discouragement fatigue.

It's the slow wear of trying again and again. Dating relationships that don't work. Long-term relationships that end in heartbreak. What Ken calls "the culture of unkindness" in so much of the dating world, the swipe apps, and the disappointment of doing it all over again. It hits hardest after what he calls stepping-stone relationships: you've done the inner work, you meet someone who seems different, and it ends the same way, only worse, "because their hopes were higher."

His answer isn't to try harder. It's to change what you measure. "The degree to which you uplevel the way you search for love is really the degree to which you're going to uplevel the kind of person you're going to meet." In place of "Did this one work out?", he offers three questions:

  • Am I becoming more self-treasuring?
  • Am I becoming more vulnerable?
  • Am I becoming more discriminating?

"If the answers to those questions are yes, you are on the right path." That, he says, is how you find light in the middle of the tunnel, not just at the end of it.

The wave of distancing

The second pattern is the one Ken calls "the worst saboteur of healthy new love that exists." If you're used to people who are not quite available, then the moment you meet someone who is truly present, your attraction can suddenly drop. "All of a sudden you notice their nose hair. You notice that their laugh irritates you. You notice that your sexual desire diminishes." In his experience, between a third and a half of all people who date go through it, and "nobody's taught to deal with it."

His guidance: expect it, and don't let it make the decision for you. He borrows a line from Marianne Williamson: "both feet in until both feet out." With someone truly available, he says, "you will be afraid, you will be nervous, you'll want to escape," but "it passes if you let the love deepen and it's the right person."

The one question to date by

Attraction matters, Ken says, but it shouldn't come first. His central question: "Does my soul feel safe with this person? Frame your entire search for love around that question and watch what changes." When your soul feels safe with someone who is present, available, and mutually attracted, "that's the happiness you could glide on almost forever."

He's also direct about two things that stall progress no matter how much inner work you've done: active addiction, and serious psychiatric conditions that haven't been stabilized. Get help with those first, he says, or "you're going to tread the same ground again and again."

Your scariest ask is your core gift

Christina shared a story from her own love life. Ken had urged her to ask a partner a question she was afraid to ask. She resisted all evening, then asked. Whatever the answer, the relief was immediate, and the relationship got more honest.

Ken's reading of that moment is the heart of his Deeper Dating approach, which centers on naming and honoring your core gifts: "The things we're most afraid to share and most afraid to ask for not only are often the most important things, they are our deepest core gifts." And: "The parts of ourselves we leave behind in order to get love or approval are the parts of ourselves we need to champion and reclaim in order to really find healthy love."

Christina put the flip side plainly: "The true feeling of abandonment, I've found, is when I abandon myself."

How this fits WeDeepen's approach

Ken's work lines up closely with WeDeepen's premise that love is a trainable skill. The Four Pillars say the same thing in different words: growth comes first, with no attachment to outcome; you own your own experience; and all feelings are welcome, including the fear that shows up when someone good arrives. Both Ken and Christina stress support: nobody gets better at love alone. That's why WeDeepen runs a weekly live session and community and Love Immersion retreats in Austin. To practice with others, join the membership. Come play with us.

FAQ

Who is Ken Page?

Ken Page, LCSW, is a psychotherapist, the author of Deeper Dating, host of the Deeper Dating Podcast, and a member of WeDeepen's faculty.

What is discouragement fatigue?

It's the exhaustion that builds from repeated dating disappointments, breakups, and unkindness, a term one of Ken Page's readers coined. He suggests measuring progress by whether you're becoming more self-treasuring, vulnerable, and discriminating, not by whether each relationship lasts.

What is the wave of distancing?

Ken Page's term for losing attraction or wanting to escape just as you meet someone truly available. He estimates it affects between a third and a half of people who date, and says it usually passes if you stay present and the person is right for you.

What question does Ken Page recommend asking when dating?

"Does my soul feel safe with this person?" He suggests framing your whole search for love around it, alongside attraction.

Where can I listen to the full episode?

Episode 106 is on the WeDeepen podcast page, Apple Podcasts, and YouTube.

pages.title: Kimi Inch on Conscious Kink: Safety, Play, and Desire
pages.short_answer: On episode 108 of Christina Weber's podcast, Austin somatic therapist Kimi Inch, founder of &More, explains conscious kink as consensual, creative play built on attunement. Her keys: a regulated nervous system comes before pleasure, every exercise is an invitation you can decline, and desire is learned in the body, not from a book. Christina shares what she learned at Kimi's four-day immersion.
pages.meta_description: Kimi Inch on conscious kink: nervous-system safety, consent as invitation, and learning the Erotic Blueprints in your body. Key ideas from episode 108.
pages.content_html:
Kimi Inch is a somatic therapist, Core Energetics practitioner, and founder of &More, an erotic leadership brand based in Austin. She is also on WeDeepen's faculty. In episode 108 of Christina Weber's podcast, recorded at Kimi's Austin home, the two walked through Something More, Kimi's four-day immersion in conscious kink, which Christina had just finished. This guide sums up what they said about safety, play, and learning desire in your body instead of from a book. Quotes are from the episode transcript, lightly edited for readability.

Kink is play, not a stereotype

Many people say "I'm not kinky." Christina's follow-up question: do you like to play? To her, kink is "novel, it's play, it's experimenting with what's possible and feeling into my emotions."

Kimi says it makes sense that people feel nervous, because the media mostly shows "this really cliche, dark, heavy, intense" picture. What she wants to bring forward is "imagination and creativity." Her playful rewrite of the stereotype: "Instead of blood, sweat, and tears, can't we just do grace and elegance instead?"

Kink names, like the one Christina took on this year, "Your Majesty," are part of the play. Kimi describes them as one instrument in an inner symphony: "Sometimes you want to give that violin a solo."

Safety starts in the nervous system

Christina asked what someone should do if they crave deeper intimacy but don't yet feel safe enough to explore it. Kimi's answer was about the body, not technique. "If we are struggling to keep a regulated nervous system, it's really hard for us to step into our pleasure and to be in deep connection and intimacy with another."

The fix is gradual exposure in a well-held setting, whether that's a therapist, a coach, or "a well-organized, conscious event where people can hold a container." Each time you're vulnerable and nothing bad happens, your nervous system learns, "I can be heard, and people can be present with me, and I won't be judged or rejected or shamed." That, she says, "opens you up to infinite possibility around pleasure and relational experiences."

Christina sees herself as proof. After years of practices like eye gazing in Tantra and connection workshops, what once felt edgy now feels easy, and each layer she goes deeper shows her a new one.

Everything is an invitation

Kimi opens every immersion with one agreement: "Everything is just a series of invitations. There's no expectation, there's no demand." You choose your own pace, and you can stop or change your mind at any time. She also asks the group to "celebrate everything," including trying an exercise for five seconds and deciding it isn't for you.

She pushes back on the idea that erotic spaces require you to be cool and polished: "We really want to encourage realness and rawness and vulnerability over this performance sort of sexy image." Christina noted that about half the group came as couples and half were currently single, and that the space honored both: "We're relationshipping in community."

Learning desire in the body

Day two of Something More centered on the Erotic Blueprints, a framework created by sex educator Jaiya that sorts arousal styles into five types: Energetic, Sensual, Sexual, Kinky, and Shapeshifter. Blueprint coach Kayce Neill taught the framework, and Kimi built a hands-on exercise for each type.

Her reason is simple: "I can attribute every successful erotic encounter with the ability of how attuned me and my partner are to ourselves and to each other." Reading about attunement isn't the same as feeling it. "Most of the time people just don't know what's possible in their lives until they actually have an experience of it. It's all theory until then."

Christina's own results changed with experience. Her first quiz months earlier put her in one type, and she felt boxed in. After the immersion she retook it and came out a Shapeshifter, which felt right. She now sees a primary blueprint as "a gateway into all of the others." Day three moved into rope work (shibari) and impact play, taught by professionals and framed as ways to practice surrender, leading, and trust.

Why this matters for your love life

Christina's point running through the episode: sex education stops at age 13, and adults rarely get a second chance. "Relationship education is something that is never ending and unfolding." That's WeDeepen's premise too. Love is a trainable skill, all feelings are welcome, and you own your own experience at every step. Practice works best repeated over time, not crammed into one weekend. WeDeepen's membership gives you a weekly live session and a community to keep practicing in, and Love Immersion retreats in Austin offer an in-person reset. Join the membership. Come play with us.

FAQ

Who is Kimi Inch?

Kimi Inch is an Austin-based somatic therapist, Core Energetics practitioner, and founder of &More, who teaches conscious kink and erotic leadership. She is on WeDeepen's faculty.

What is conscious kink?

As Kimi Inch describes it, conscious kink is consensual erotic play built on attunement, care, and choice, where every activity is an invitation you can accept, decline, or stop at any time.

What are the five Erotic Blueprint types?

Energetic, Sensual, Sexual, Kinky, and Shapeshifter. The framework was created by Jaiya. Most people are a mix of all five, with one or two leading.

Do you need a partner to explore this kind of work?

No. In the immersion Christina attended, about half the participants came as couples and half were currently single.

Where can I listen to the full episode?

Episode 108 is on the WeDeepen podcast page, Apple Podcasts, and YouTube. For Kimi's background, listen to episode 99, Beyond the Whip.
